inline.s: such a person is the foremost and most rare
this person has no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of beings, no mark of a life span

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. The circulating edition and the early Qing edition read: 'This person has no mark of self, no mark of a person, no mark of beings, no mark of a life span.')
then it is called all Buddhas

(The Liushu through the Zhang copy, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition and the Ming-Qing engravings, the 'then' (ze) is written 'namely' (ji).)
it is not the foremost paramita
(The Liushu through the Ming engraving and the Hui commentary recension are all the same. The circulating edition and the early Qing edition read 'namely not' (ji fei).)
the Tathagata speaks of the paramita of patience that is not

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving and the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition and the early Qing edition, beneath this sentence is added the sentence 'this is named the paramita of patience.' Some early Qing editions note beneath it: 'The sentence of naming is absent in the old editions, yet it cannot be omitted.' From this it can be seen that it was added at that time. According to the Master Zhi commentary [Zhi shu]: 'Since there is already no self and no other, who applies it and who endures? Thus patience that is not patience is patience, practiced as not-patience, which is the body of prajna.' The Essential Selections [Zuan Yao] says: 'Patience reaching the other shore has already left the mark of suffering; how much more so since the other shore is no shore at all: who suffers and who endures?' Among all the other old commentaries there is none that contains the meaning of the sentence of naming.)
then it is not dwelling

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving, and the Hui commentary, the Zhao commentary, the Master Zhi commentary, the Essential Selections and the four-recension edition are all the same. In the circulating edition and the early Qing edition the 'then' is written 'namely'.)
the bodhisattva for the sake of benefiting all beings

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving and the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition beneath 'beings' there is the character 'therefore' [gu], which was added in the early Qing period. Some early Qing editions note beneath it: 'The various editions do not have the character "therefore".')
then it is not beings

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Ming engraving and the Hui-Zhao combined commentary recension are all the same. In the circulating edition and the early Qing edition the 'then' is written 'namely'. The Southern Tang stone print and the Zhang copy are likewise.)
then there is no view of self

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions, and the circulating edition are all the same. This with the passages below, 'then it is the Tathagata who with Buddha wisdom,' 'then it is the one who bears the burden,' 'then it is a stupa for this sutra,' 'then it is extinguished,' in the early Qing edition the 'then' is frequently written 'namely'.)
all accomplishing immeasurable, incalculable, boundless, inconceivable merit

(The Liushu has it thus; the other editions read 'all attaining' [jie de cheng jiu]. According to the Hui commentary: 'If a person, relying on the sutra, puts it into practice, then immeasurable blessings arise, corresponding to the three Buddha natures; therefore he can perfect the realm-seeds. Realm [jie] means true thusness; seeds [zhong] mean the bodhi mind and the practice of the six perfections. Realm-seeds are the three Buddha natures.' Pondering this commentary, we can know it has no character 'attain' [de]. 'Attain' means 'will attain.' Now, saying that it corresponds to the three Buddha natures means that it is already accomplished. 'Already accomplished' means that its accomplishment of correspondence means it already possesses the material that can perfect the realm-seeds; it does not mean that it has already become a Buddha. This is what the Changshui record says: 'If one can proclaim and uphold it, then this is the twofold practice of benefit to self and others, able to keep the Buddha-seed from being cut off, and is called bearing the burden of bodhi.' The word 'accomplish' thus speaks of accomplishing the bearing of the burden. Therefore the Changshui record also says: 'The immeasurable and other merits serve as the cause of supreme bodhi.' On this basis, it sufficiently proves that the original text had no character 'attain'.)
the mind then becomes frantic and confused

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition and the early Qing edition the 'then' is written 'namely'.)
one who arouses the mind of anuttara samyaksambodhi

(The Liushu is thus. In the other editions above the character 'one who' [zhe] there is the character 'mind' [xin]. According to the purport of the sutra, it is precisely refuting the mind that holds to a dharma of bodhi; therefore immediately below it closely follows: 'one should give rise to the thought thus: I should cause all beings to attain nirvana, even to the thought that no being is brought to nirvana.' Then under 'bodhi' one cannot attach the character 'mind'. The point is made clear by the Tang dynasty manuscripts; the same for below.)
why, if a bodhisattva has a mark of self, a mark of others, a mark of beings, a mark of a life span, then he is not a bodhisattva

(The Liushu, the Ming engraving and the Hui edition are all the same. The Weng copy and on to the circulating edition have the three characters 'Subhuti' above 'if'. Also the early Qing edition writes 'namely not' for 'then not'.)
in truth there is no dharma by which one who arouses anuttara samyaksambodhi...
(The Liushu is thus. In the other editions above the character 'one who' there is the character 'mind'.)
if there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attains anuttara samyaksambodhi
(The Liushu edition and the Hui edition are the same. In the other editions beneath 'bodhi' there is the character 'one who' [zhe].)
then Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy
(The ancient and modern editions are all the same. In the early Qing edition the 'then' is written 'namely'.)
then it is not the great body

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Zhang copy, the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition the 'then' is written 'namely'. The Weng copy and the early Qing edition are likewise.)
then he is not called a bodhisattva
there is no dharma that is called a bodhisattva

(The Liushu, the Hui edition and the Zhao edition are all the same. The circulating edition reads 'in truth there is none' [shi wu]. The Southern Tang stone print and after are all so. According to the Changshui record: 'It is only that, free of self and free of others, true thusness is pure, and is called a bodhisattva; it does not speak of a separate dharma.' This sufficiently proves the original had no character 'in truth' [shi]. If it had it, it would say 'it is not speaking of a dharma that truly exists,' and not say 'separate.')
all the sands in the Ganges

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Zhang copy and the Hui edition are all the same. In the circulating edition above 'Ganges' there is the character 'such' [ru]. The Southern Tang stone print and the Ming-Qing editions are likewise.)
